title: Even Rome: not every 'divine faith' assent equals Catholic dogmatic certainty — Catharinus & Vasquez
source_text: CXXXIX. Et certe non solum inter Reformatos, sed in ipsa Schola Romana, non quicunque assensus ad fidem divinam refertur, hoc ipso statim aequatur firmitate & certitudine cum assensu fidei Catholicae, sive dogmaticae. Nam in ipso Concilio Tridentino Catharinus contendit hominem justum fide divina certum esse posse de propria gratia. Et Vasquez quoque Jesuita fidem divinam vocat, fiduciam quam peccator poenitens habet de venia a Deo impetranda, & quam homo justificatus potest habere de illa impetrata. Nec tamen isti viri putant illam privatam fidem, parem habere cum fide Catholica certitudinem. Et ad Catharini sententiam respexit Concilium Tridentinum, dum definiens, quod nullus scire valeat certitudine fidei, se gratiam Dei esse consecutum, post verbum illud fidei inserit, cui non potest subesse falsum, ut aliqua evadendi rima Catharino superesset, nec videretur simpliciter Decreto Concilii damnatus. Ut & revera post Canonem illum in sententia priori perstitit, & conatus est verba Concilii, secundum suum sensum, interpretari.
pass_a_gloss: And certainly not only among the Reformed, but in the Roman School itself, not every assent that is referred to divine faith is by that very fact at once equaled in firmness and certainty with the assent of Catholic or dogmatic faith. For in the Council of Trent itself Catharinus contended that a just man can be certain by divine faith concerning his own grace. And Vasquez the Jesuit also calls divine faith the fiducia which a penitent sinner has concerning pardon to be obtained from God, and which a justified man can have concerning that pardon already obtained. Yet those men do not think that that private faith has equal certainty with Catholic faith. And the Council of Trent had regard to Catharinus's opinion when, defining that no one can know with the certainty of faith that he has obtained the grace of God, it inserted after that word of faith the phrase to which falsehood cannot be subject, so that some crack of escape might remain for Catharinus, and he might not seem simply condemned by the Council's Decree. As indeed after that Canon he persisted in his prior opinion and tried to interpret the Council's words according to his own sense.
pass_b_english: Even inside the Roman school, not every assent labeled divine faith matches Catholic dogmatic certainty.

At Trent, Catharinus held a just man can be divinely certain of his own grace; Vasquez calls divine faith both the penitent's trust of pardon-to-come and the justified man's trust of pardon obtained — yet neither equates that private faith with Catholic certainty.

Trent's canon that none can know with faith-certainty he has obtained grace added 'to which falsehood cannot be subject' with an eye to Catharinus — who afterward still kept his view and re-read the decree.

rejected: Rome uniformly equates all divine-faith assents
